title: Beowulf
author: Anonymous
openingChapterLabel: Fitt I — The Life and Death of Scyld
openingText: Lo! the Spear-Danes’ glory through splendid achievements / The folk-kings’ former fame we have heard of, / How princes displayed then their prowess-in-battle. / Oft Scyld the Scefing from scathers in numbers / From many a people their mead-benches tore. / Since first he found him friendless and wretched, / The earl had had terror: comfort he got for it, / Waxed ’neath the welkin, world-honor gained, / Till all his neighbors o’er sea were compelled to / Bow to his bidding and bring him their tribute: / An excellent atheling!
about:
Beowulf is the oldest surviving epic in the English language — a poem composed somewhere between the seventh and tenth centuries, telling a story that feels even older. A Geatish warrior named Beowulf crosses the sea to Denmark, kills the monster Grendel with his bare hands, then kills Grendel’s mother in the depths of a black mere. Decades later, as an aging king, he faces a fire-breathing dragon alone and dies doing it. The poem ends with his funeral pyre on a clifftop and his warriors riding around the mound, singing.

Tolkien spent decades studying Beowulf before writing The Lord of the Rings. Much of what feels ancient and inevitable in modern fantasy — the mead-hall, the ring-giver, the hero who must die, the world that darkens after him — traces back here. This is the bedrock. Reading it is reading the origin.

angleCards.title: The heroic code in action.
angleCards.text: Beowulf operates by a precise set of rules: boast before battle, fight with your own hands, give your treasures away, never flinch. Every speech is a declaration of what he owes and what he is owed. This is ethics as honor, and it runs entirely on reputation.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the Germanic heroic code — the obligations of lord and thane, the logic of boasting and gift-giving — and what kind of life it demands of the man who lives by it.

angleCards.title: Pagan world, Christian poem.
angleCards.text: Beowulf’s world is full of fate, glory, and doom — yet the poet is Christian, and keeps interrupting with references to Cain, God’s creation, and Providence. The two frameworks sit uneasily together. Watching where they collide is one of the poem’s deepest pleasures.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Beowulf as a text in transition — a pagan heroic world refracted through a Christian poet’s lens, and what that double vision reveals about both.

angleCards.title: Three monsters, one arc.
angleCards.text: Grendel is brute force in the dark. Grendel’s Mother is grief turned to vengeance. The dragon is ancient, patient, and provoked by a single theft. The three fights are not repetitions — they chart Beowulf’s whole life: young strength, maturity, and the death that no hero escapes.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the poem as a three-act meditation on the shape of a heroic life — what youth, middle age, and old age each demand of a man who refuses to step back.

angleCards.title: The outsider defines the tribe.
angleCards.text: Grendel is exiled from the hall, excluded from the feast, cursed to wander the marshes alone. The poem defines what is human — warmth, community, song, gift-exchange — by showing what Grendel cannot be. He is not evil so much as irreparably outside.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Grendel as the poem’s mirror — understanding how the poem defines heroic society by the creature it casts out, and what that tells us about belonging and exclusion.

cast.name: Beowulf
cast.description: The strongest man alive, nephew of King Hygelac. He comes to Denmark not because he must but because he can — and because reputation is the only thing that outlasts a man.

cast.name: Grendel
cast.description: A descendant of Cain, cursed by God and cast into the wilderness. He is tormented by the sound of joy in Heorot and takes his revenge on it, night after night, for twelve years.

cast.name: Grendel’s Mother
cast.description: After Beowulf tears her son’s arm away, she strikes back. More calculating than Grendel and harder to kill, she draws Beowulf into her world — the bottom of a black mere — to settle the debt.

cast.name: Hrothgar
cast.description: Builder of Heorot, the greatest mead-hall in the world, and the man who has watched it be emptied every night for twelve years. He is old, helpless against Grendel, and still great enough to recognize a hero when one arrives.

cast.name: Wiglaf
cast.description: Of all Beowulf’s thanes, only Wiglaf refuses to flee when the dragon’s fire proves too much. He charges through the flames to stand beside his lord — and becomes the poem’s image of what loyalty actually requires.

cast.name: The Dragon
cast.description: Three hundred years old, coiled over a buried treasure in a stone barrow. When a fugitive steals a single cup, the dragon burns the Geatish countryside to ash — and Beowulf, now an old king, decides to face it alone.
